clue.text: Highlights Bill and his money

parts.note: AC is the short form of account, a bill
Bill read as an American's name, whose small change comes in cents

explanation.surface: Somebody's bank statements, with Bill and his cash marked out in highlighter.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill does double duty in the surface as a man's name, but it is the account abbreviation; 'his money' leans on the American flavour of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: To accent something is to stress it, and a verb meaning stresses or emphasises matches highlights used as a verb.

clue.text: President Trump's inauguration covered by "overfill" — it would take place here

parts.note: George Washington, the first US President

indicators.note: something covered by another sits inside it, so the following word wraps around the kept letter

parts.note: to sate is to fill to excess

indicators.note: an inauguration is a beginning, so only the opening letter of the word Trump's is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: A satirical swipe at Trump's swearing-in ceremony being stuffed to bursting.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful one: the clue imagines the inauguration happening in Washington, and the answer is the state sharing that name rather than the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue jokes that the ceremony belongs in a place named after the first president, and the Pacific Northwest state carries exactly that name.

clue.text: 'Touch up Chuck', played by unwelcome company

parts.note: to goose someone is to grope or prod them
Chuck Berry, the rock and roll guitarist

explanation.surface: A song called 'Touch up Chuck' being performed by a band nobody wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' looks like a verb meaning throw, but it is the first name of Chuck Berry, whose surname is needed. 'Played by' fits the musician image while only joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In British idiom, to play gooseberry is to be the unwanted third person tagging along with a courting couple.

clue.text: see 22ac.
Needing a lot of workers, party, deeply emotional, recruits … four

parts.note: the UK Labour Party

indicators.note: to recruit is to take someone in, so the preceding word enlists the next one inside itself

parts.note: intense feelings run deep
Roman numeral for four

explanation.surface: A political party, in an emotional state, is hiring staff for a job that takes many hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis before 'four' makes it look like a trailing thought, but it is just the Roman numeral to be taken in.
explanation.definitionFit: A labour-intensive process demands much human effort and therefore many employees, rather than machines or capital.

clue.text: Start to stroke thigh — shit, it'll get you in a lather

definitions.text: it'll get you in a lather

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letter of stroke is used

parts.note: first letter
the ham is the back of the thigh
a coarse word and a childish word for the same thing

explanation.surface: An erotic massage takes a messy turn that leaves someone very agitated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a lather' usually means flustered, which the surface invites; the definition reads it literally as foam on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair wash is rubbed into the scalp and foams up, literally covering you in suds.

clue.text: Leather makes me pretentious when Prince is about

indicators.note: being about something means surrounding it, so the royal's name goes round the other piece

parts.note: Chas is a short form of Charles, as in Prince Charles
the French moi is a pretentious way of saying me

explanation.surface: Someone feels affected and posh whenever royalty is nearby, and wears leather to show it.
explanation.walkthrough: MOI is the knowingly affected French way to say me, as Miss Piggy does.
explanation.definitionFit: Chamois is a soft pliable leather made from the skin of a mountain goat or sheep, used for polishing.

clue.text: It's not observed much now, Bab's fancy new hat

indicators.note: something fancy is elaborate and made over, so the name before it is rearranged

parts.note: letters of the name with its s

indicators.note: a new version is a remodelled one, so the word after it is rearranged too

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Babs shows off an elaborate new hat, of the kind seldom worn these days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Observed' looks like 'seen', so the hat seems to be the thing rarely noticed; it means kept, as a holy day is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: The weekly day of rest is a religious observance that relatively few people keep strictly in modern secular life.

clue.text: Blow on right of organ's blinking hair

indicators.note: placed on the right of means written after, setting the order of the two pieces

parts.note: the eye is a sense organ
a lash is a stroke of a whip

explanation.surface: Someone hit on the right side of a body part, with mild cursing about some hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blinking' reads as a British mild swear word, like bloody, but here it describes a hair that literally blinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the short hairs fringing the eyelid moves every time you close and open the eye.

clue.text: Boner shown by topless rogue

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter of the word that follows is lost

parts.note: a little terror is a rascal or rogue

explanation.surface: A smutty scene of a bare-chested scoundrel and an aroused onlooker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boner' is chosen for its rude sense, but it is also slang for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A boner, in informal American usage, is a stupid mistake or howler.

clue.text: Moral significance confuses the Tories — no tie, right?

indicators.note: confusing a group muddles it, so the remaining letters are jumbled
no signals the absence of what follows, so those letters must be taken out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, to be removed
R is the abbreviation for right, also removed

explanation.surface: Political sketch: tieless Tories bewildered by questions of morality.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the letters of tie and one R from the Tories, then jumble the five left.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the guiding moral character or spirit of a group, the values that give it meaning.

clue.text: Veto Johnson's last outburst to go after voters

parts.note: to bar is to forbid

indicators.note: the last of a name is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: final letter of the name
a storm of protest is an outburst

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson blocks something, throws a final tantrum, then goes campaigning.
explanation.definitionFit: To barnstorm is to tour an area making rousing speeches, originally in barns, to win votes.

clue.text: Brainy lot spun for him!

indicators.note: spinning turns things round, so the letters before it are rearranged; spin doctors also suit the politician

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A clever team of spin doctors working on behalf of a leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue evokes the New Labour spin machine of Alastair Campbell and Peter Mandelson, which is why 'him' is enough to point at the man.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for the former Labour prime minister whose government was famous for its media manipulators.

clue.text: see 21dn.
Observing: "Grasping Tone's worried"

parts.note: grasping something is taking hold of it

indicators.note: worried things are troubled and shaken, so the name before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An onlooker quotes a remark that someone called Tone is anxious and greedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying attention to something and registering it is a synonym phrase for watching or noticing.

clue.text: Stiffen when arse's flipped with chain

indicators.note: flipping something turns it end over end, so the word before is read backwards

parts.note: both are exclamations of annoyance
CH is the abbreviation for chain, an old unit of length

explanation.surface: Someone's backside is tipped over and chained up, leaving them rigid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arse' looks like the body part, but it is the cry 'Arse!', which means the same as 'Rats!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Laundry starch is applied to collars and shirts to make the fabric firm, so the verb means to make rigid.

clue.text: Not much concealed by this nuclear test site

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a skimpy two-piece swimsuit
second meaning: the Pacific atoll where the US tested atomic bombs

explanation.surface: A tongue-in-cheek line about very little being hidden at a weapons proving ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The swimsuit was named after the atoll, supposedly because its effect would be explosive.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marshall Islands atoll hosted American atomic tests, and the brief two-piece swimwear covers little of the body.

clue.text: Bollocks trail after symbolic animal

parts.note: bull is slang for nonsense, as is bollocks
to dog someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: A crude retort to a suggestion of tracking a national mascot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bollocks' reads as an anatomical word, but it is meant as rubbish or nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: This stocky breed is the traditional emblem of Britain, representing stubbornness and the nation's character.

clue.text: Show for Mussolini?

parts.note: pro means in favour of
Il Duce was Mussolini's title

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about which spectacle was staged for the Italian dictator.
explanation.definitionFit: To produce something is to bring it out and display it, as when producing a ticket for inspection.

clue.text: University adversary finally interrupts Greer broadcast — "it's cheesy"

indicators.note: interrupting breaks into the middle, so the first pieces go inside the scattered name
broadcast seed is scattered, so the surname is strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the final letter of adversary is used

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: An academic opponent heckles Germaine Greer on air with a jibe that her talk is corny.
explanation.walkthrough: Germaine Greer is the Australian feminist writer and broadcaster. 'Broadcast' suggests a homophone, but here it scatters the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gruyère is a Swiss cheese, so the joke reading of cheesy as 'made of cheese' fits it literally.

clue.text: Eager to screw top off drink

indicators.note: taking the top off removes the first letter of the word that follows

parts.note: brandy is a spirit

explanation.surface: Someone keen to twist the cap off a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw top' looks like a bottle cap, but the definition ends at 'screw', used in its sexual sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Randy is informal British slang for sexually aroused, keen for intercourse.

clue.text: Helping hand from wanton true love gripping middle of penis

wanton means unruly and undisciplined, so the following words are disordered

clue.text: Support produces very painful outburst

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for very
the cry when something hurts

explanation.definitionFit: To vouch for someone is to back them up or guarantee their character, a verb of endorsement.

clue.text: Job by Spring? Much obliged!

parts.note: a duty is a task
to spring is to leap or bound

explanation.surface: A grateful reply to someone offering work by springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Much obliged' is normally a way of saying thank you; here it means strongly compelled.
explanation.definitionFit: Being duty-bound means being morally or legally required to do something, heavily compelled.

clue.text: Poor Gove, tense inside — er, put it behind you!

something in poor shape is out of order, so the surname is rearranged

parts.note: Michael Gove, the Conservative politician

taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells an anxious, hesitant Michael Gove to move on from a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Gove is a long-serving British Conservative minister. 'Tense' looks like an adjective describing him, but it is the grammatical term.
